item.title: How COP31 became climate diplomacy’s ‘darkest moment’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: comprehensive coverage of a significant climate event

No one expected the 31st Conference of the Parties to be game-changing — from the start, everyone called it an “implementation” COP — but those gathered in Antalya, Turkey, hoped it would at least maintain momentum on clean energy development. They also wanted to see countries reaffirm their commitment to multilateral climate action amid heightened geopolitical tension.

Instead, the talks collapsed after two weeks of negotiations that ran nearly 50 hours into overtime — longer than ever before. More than 90 nations, including the Marshall Islands, the United Kingdom, and the entire European Union, objected to a draft of the high-level political agreement, called a cover decision, that typically caps each COP because it omitted the words “fossil fuels” and left key details about climate finance unaddressed.

“We will not endorse an Antalya pact or cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change,” Irish climate minister Darragh O’Brien said during a closing plenary. “The draft put before us does not begin to address the climate emergency that we face, and therefore the EU cannot accept it.”

In an unusual arrangement, this year’s negotiations were run by ministers from Turkey and Australia. It was the first climate conference since COP15 in 2009 to founder over a cover decision, something many nations blamed on shoddy management by the hosts.

This time, the breakdown came at a time of even greater peril. The world is being racked by extreme heat, raging wildfires, and devastating floods, and it is on the brink of permanently exceeding 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) of warming, a threshold long at the center of climate diplomacy. A historic El Niño stands to intensify those impacts.

Yet countries could not reach consensus on some of the most fundamental questions about how to address the crisis. Beyond the disagreements over fossil fuels and climate finance, delegates clashed over carbon capture, a call to have electricity meet 35 percent of the world’s energy needs, and the timing of a major scientific report on climate change.

As diplomats left Antalya, observers described the outcome in unusually dire terms, calling it “the worst COP ever” and “one of the darkest hours in the history of climate negotiations.” The failure has intensified a longstanding question about the U.N. climate process: Can a system that requires nearly 200 countries to reach consensus still deliver meaningful action — or will countries willing to move faster act outside of it?

“The lack of consensus … cannot be delinked from global geopolitics, where nationalism and protectionism seem to upend multilateralism,” Ali Mohamed, a lead negotiator for a bloc of African countries, wrote in a message to Grist. “The ongoing conflicts and the breakdown of international rules-based order have further emboldened disregard of common global agenda even in the face of real and science-backed facts.”

Here’s why the talks collapsed, and where global climate action goes from here.

Opposition from petrostates

Fossil fuels were one of the biggest points of contention. While countries agreed three years ago at COP28 to transition away from fossil fuels, this year Saudi Arabia, Russia, and other petrostates blocked any affirmation of that commitment, including through alternative language about the “transition toward low greenhouse gas emissions and climate resilience.”

In the end, the COP presidents’ final proposal only briefly mentioned “recalling” COP28 without specifying what part of it was being recalled.

Fossil fuel-producing countries also blocked language that would have established a target of generating 35 percent of the world’s energy from electricity by 2035 — up from 23 percent today — while reaffirming efforts to deploy renewable energy and prevent methane leaks. Turkish environmental minister Murat Kurum had pitched the electrification pledge as a smart strategic move in the wake of the Iran war, which blocked petroleum products from moving through the Strait of Hormuz. More than 130 nations, including members of the EU, the Alliance of Small Island States, and the Least Developed Countries, backed the pledge before it was scuttled.

“The interests of a few were allowed to obstruct the ambition needed by many,” said Wopke Hoekstra, the European Union’s lead climate negotiator, in a statement at the close of the talks.

A focus on the ‘cover decision‘

In past U.N. climate summits, negotiators have battled over multiple agreements covering issues like adaptation and finance. This year, the Australian and Turkish diplomats running the talks focused most of their energy on the cover decision, an overarching agreement meant to summarize the state of climate action — even as countries like Russia rejected the very idea of a summary document.

“There has never been a cover decision that was the object of so much focus by the presidency, ministers, and negotiators that has been so resoundingly rejected by a significant group of countries,” said Alden Meyer, a senior associate at the climate-focused think tank E3G and a veteran of U.N. climate talks.

The haggling sapped attention from negotiations over other issues, said Imane Saidi, a senior researcher at the Imal Initiative for Climate and Development and a climate finance negotiator.

“Developed countries came to this COP with no desired outcome,” she said. “They are not really looking to land anything specific. “A cover decision is kind of by definition a package, so that means that it will lower the ambition, and it will be kind of the lowest denominator.”

item.title: The world doesn’t need solar or wind — it needs both
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: useful information on energy grid diversification

Humans are still hunter-gatherers — not for food, but for energy. Much like we once roamed the landscape digging up edible roots, today we gouge the planet for coal, oil, and gas. But just as we eventually adopted agriculture, we’re starting to farm the wind and sun. Because we can’t stop our star from setting, though, we must combine solar panels with large batteries, which load up on energy during the day and distribute it at night.

According to a new report from the energy think tank Ember, diversifying the electrical grid by adding wind power is a massive opportunity to reduce costs. “If you rely on one crop and that crop is having a bad year, you’re going to be struggling,” said Daan Walter, principal at Ember and author of the new report. “The same is true for wind and solar, and it’s the reason why diversification is so important. We’re now building batteries, and those are effectively the silos where we store the sunshine for later in the day.”

The report found that in the United States and Europe, you’d need 20 hours of battery storage to achieve 90 percent uptime for solar. Add wind power to the system and that drops to just 12 hours, meaning you don’t have to install as many costly lithium-ion batteries. Accordingly, worldwide this technique could drop the median cost of meeting that 90 percent demand from $105 per megawatt-hour with solar to $86 with additional wind power. (You can see the potential of that wind power in the map below — it alone can more than meet electricity demand.)

One of the challenges with solar power is the planet’s pesky seasons. If you’re at the equator, you bask in sunlight all year round, bathing your panels in constant rays. In that case, you don’t really need wind power, if you have a lot of panels plugged into batteries.

Move farther north or south, though, and you’re getting much less solar power as the winter drags on. To ensure that everyone’s getting enough juice during those dark days, you’d need lots of batteries and what are called “long-duration energy storage” techniques. These include pumped storage hydropower, in which you use wind or solar power to pump water uphill into a reservoir, then release it to spin turbines when you need electricity, giving you a bigger (and longer lasting) surplus of energy than with lithium-ion batteries.

Now imagine northern grids that hum with plenty of solar power in the long days of summer, but can also exploit the wind in the long nights of winter. In the map above, you’ll see the savings from combining the two are greatest in the northern parts of the planet. The report found that without wind, solar and batteries can achieve 90 percent uptime near the equator for less than $60 per megawatt-hour, in contrast to areas above 55 degrees north costing $280. Add wind to the mix and at every latitude, the costs dip below $100.

“At least from a cost perspective and a reliability perspective, you can have clean power at competitive enough prices,” said Al-Amin Bugaje, a research fellow studying the electrical sector at the climate solutions nonprofit Project Drawdown, who wasn’t involved in the research. That means not having to keep developing fossil fuel power infrastructure.

Combining solar and wind could also help ward off the dreaded dunkelflaute — literally, “dark doldrums,” from the German — also known as anticyclonic gloom. These are extended periods where there’s simultaneously too little sun and too little wind, which is obviously a problem for panels and turbines. The Ember analysis finds that on average across the world, this lull for solar happens about four times a year, and for wind around eight. “That’s very annoying, because then you need to store lots of energy beforehand,” Walter said. “You need to build an awful lot of batteries to actually get that done.”

That, of course, raises costs. But, Walter found, by combining wind and solar, you instead experience a dunkelflaute on average every four years. (You can see this visualized in the graph above — green and blue are solar and wind droughts, respectively, and dark blue is both happening simultaneously.) Ideally, there’d be enough battery and long-duration storage on the grid to get utilities through those stretches without having to spin up gas or coal power plants.

If you can’t relate to the farming metaphor of diversifying energy like diversifying crops, consider your retirement portfolio: Instead of buying one stock that can crash, investing in lots of companies spreads the risk. Ideally, in a few decades you’re looking at a steadily rising curve on a graph. “You want to put everything in an ETF or in an index with a basket of really good options or companies,” said Bugaje. “Over a long period of time, you’re safe that you’re going in the top right corner direction.”

Source: Grist | Published: 2026-11-23 09:45 UTC | Difficulty: 60/100

item.title: An Alabama Pipeline Exploded. Its Owner Is Fighting To Expand It.
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: detailed report on a pipeline explosion and its implications

On Saturday night, the midnight skies over west Alabama lit up as a massive fireball leaped hundreds of feet in the air, visible from more than 50 miles away.

The source of the explosion, officials later confirmed, was a segment of Southern Natural Gas Company pipeline running through rural Sumter County, about eight miles east of the Mississippi state line in Alabama’s Black Belt.

The explosion occurred at approximately 11:27 p.m. in an empty field near the unincorporated community of Ward. The blast was significant enough to be visible on weather radar, according to local meteorologists.

No injuries were reported, according to the company and local officials.

Shortly after the explosion, Mayor Renee Ward Pringle of nearby York, population 2,400, said she’d heard from many residents asking about the seemingly apocalyptic views of a massive blaze on the horizon.

“We understand the concerns of our citizens, especially with the light from the flames being visible from York,” Pringle wrote on social media. “While the preliminary information is encouraging, we do not want to make any premature assurances regarding public safety.”

Southern Natural Gas Company is jointly owned by Kinder Morgan and Southern Company and operated by Kinder Morgan. The company operates about 7,000 miles of pipelines distributing fossil gas throughout the Southeast, including to major gas-fired power plants operated by Southern Company and its subsidiaries, Alabama Power, Georgia Power and Mississippi Power.

Kinder Morgan described the explosion as a force majeure incident, meaning the company claims the incident was caused by circumstances beyond human control, which it characterized as “a natural gas release and fire on a pipeline segment.” No further information on the cause of the explosion has been released as of Monday afternoon.

In response to questions about the explosion, the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration confirmed to Inside Climate News that its staff has been deployed to the site of the pipeline failure and that the agency’s investigation is ongoing.

Portia Shepherd, executive director of the environmental justice nonprofit Blackbelt Women Rising, said she sees the explosion as a warning shot.

“This could have happened in any community along this pipeline,” Shepherd said. “These explosions are happening again and again, and they want to expand.”

Federal regulators issued orders forcing SNG to take corrective actions following explosions along other sections of the pipeline in 2022 and 2026, records show.

Still, SNG plans to expand the pipeline at issue as part of a multi-billion project called South System Expansion 4 that would increase the company’s pipeline capacity by about 1.3 billion cubic feet per day—enough methane to fill nearly 15,000 Olympic-sized swimming pools.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

Shepherd and other community leaders across Alabama’s Black Belt are opposed to the expansion, which they have said will lead to increased risks for communities that are already suffering.

In October, attorneys for the Southern Environmental Law Center filed a lawsuit on behalf of impacted landowners and nine nonprofits across the South, including Shepherd’s, asking a federal court to review and set aside a ruling by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission that authorized the major methane pipeline expansion across Mississippi, Alabama and Georgia.

Megan Gibson, an attorney for SELC, said that Saturday’s explosion is a “stark reminder that the risks of building another pipeline alongside aging, existing pipelines are very real for the families and communities living along these routes.”

Gibson called on FERC to act immediately to address safety concerns raised by the incident.

“In our ongoing challenge to FERC’s approval of the massive SSE4 expansion of this aging infrastructure, we raised serious concerns about the dangers of constructing new high-pressure pipelines alongside existing lines with a history of failures—and FERC should immediately order a stop to any and all construction activities and fully examine and address these risks, including in partnership with the Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration,” Gibson said.

The explosion has also raised concerns about the passage of federal permitting legislation that would cut red tape for major energy infrastructure projects like SSE4.

“The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, or BAAJA, will fast track pipelines like this one, hindering our ability to have a voice in the process and putting more Alabama communities in immediate danger,” the Alabama Rivers Alliance, an environmental nonprofit, wrote in a statement in the wake of Saturday’s explosion.

Shepherd said she’s grateful that no one was injured in the incident, but residents in Sumter County and across the Black Belt that she’s spoken with are concerned that no comprehensive safety plans exist for when incidents like this happen. Even when limited planning is in place, she said, companies and public officials don’t do a good job of informing the public about what they should do in case of an emergency.

“Where is the plan that these communities can actually see?” Shepherd asked. “Where are the safety measures?”

In the end, Shepherd said she doesn’t believe that companies like Kinder Morgan have communities’ best interests at heart.

“These companies’ executives need to look at these communities as places where they would actually live, because I think they’d be doing a better job if these risks were in their community,” Shepherd said.

“But the reality is these discussions don’t come up in their community, because they don’t let companies do stuff like this in their communities. It’s always us. We’re the ones who get dumped on.”…

item.title: A Midwest Manufacturer Ditched a Potent Greenhouse Gas. Will Others Follow?
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: interesting case study on greenhouse gas reduction

ANDERSON, Ind.—Inside a cavernous former General Motors plant, furnaces melt scrap metal into high-purity metal ingots at one of the world’s largest magnesium recyclers.

Until recently, Advanced Magnesium Alloys Corp. was also the country’s largest emitter of sulfur hexafluoride, the most potent greenhouse gas on the planet.

In 2023, the company used 10 metric tons of the climate pollutant as a “cover gas” to prevent molten magnesium from burning. Once used, the gas was released directly into the atmosphere. The emissions from a plant with just 40 employees were equivalent to the annual greenhouse gas pollution of nearly 60,000 automobiles.

Then, in 2024, the company switched to a climate-friendly alternative. Its SF6 emissions fell to zero.

SF6 “served this industry for many years, but it’s also proven to be not very good for civilization,” said Arie Shaked, chief operations officer for Advanced Magnesium Alloys.

During a recent tour of the facility, Shaked walked past rows of freshly cooled, carefully stacked bricks of lightweight magnesium alloy that others will cast into automobile parts, such as steering wheels or car seat frames, or blend into aluminum alloys. A cloud of magnesium oxide dust rose from the open hatch of a nearby furnace as workers scrubbed the unit between production cycles.

SF6 is invisible, non-toxic and effective at preventing fires. The gas is also 24,300 times more effective at warming the atmosphere than carbon dioxide, pound for pound.

The U.S. has no federal regulations prohibiting its use in magnesium production and casting—the process of pouring or injecting molten metal into molds to form parts—and Indiana hasn’t enacted any rules of its own. But California and the European Union banned its use for those purposes roughly a decade ago.

The U.S. instead took a voluntary approach to reducing emissions. From 1999 to 2010, the Environmental Protection Agency and the International Magnesium Association worked with manufacturers to develop best practices with the goal of eliminating SF6 use by 2010. The effort included a 2008 study at Advanced Magnesium Alloys, where researchers tested alternative cover gases.

SF6 emissions from U.S. magnesium production and casting fell 74 percent between 1999 and 2010 but have since plateaued. In 2023, the most recent year for which data is available, emissions totaled 1.1 million metric tons of carbon dioxide equivalent, EPA records show. That’s equal to the annual greenhouse gas emissions of more than a quarter-million automobiles.

Before joining Advanced Magnesium Alloys, Shaked managed a magnesium planet in Israel, where he oversaw the company’s transition from SF6 to sulfur dioxide in the late 1990s and early 2000s. Although sulfur dioxide is widely used as an alternative cover gas, it is also corrosive and toxic. Drawing on that experience, Shaked was reluctant to make the same switch at the Indiana plant. The company twice tested an alternative, fluorine-based cover gas, but neither trial succeeded.

Shaked said low winter temperatures, incorrect gas mixtures or insufficient amounts of the gas may have contributed to the failures.

A few years ago the company began testing the fluorine-based gas again, initially hoping it might work for part of their process. But after experimenting with different volumes and concentrations, they found the gas, known as BestSolv Zulu, could replace SF6 throughout the plant. The company is now seeking carbon credits for its emissions reductions. It remains unclear how potential revenue from the credits will compare to the cost of the transition, Shaked said.

While Advanced Magnesium Alloys transitioned off SF6, other Midwest manufacturers, many of whom supply the automotive industry here in one of the nation’s major industrial regions, continue to rely on it.

Magnesium Products of America, a die caster in Eaton Rapids, Michigan, released 6 metric tons of SF6 in 2024, according to data the company reported to the EPA, making it the largest emitter among magnesium producers in the country that year. However, the company also used about 7 metric tons of an alternative, climate-friendly cover gas, allowing it to reduce the amount of SF6 it would otherwise have needed.

Jonathan Weiler, chief engineer for Meridian Lightweight Technologies, its parent company, confirmed the figures and said the company aims to eliminate routine use of the climate pollutant at its Michigan facility within three to five years. The company also operates plants in Canada, where it reduced SF6 use by more than 90 percent since 2023, said Weiler, who is also the president of the International Magnesium Association.

Terves, a magnesium and aluminum alloys producer in Euclid, Ohio, emitted 3.7 metric tons of SF6 in 2024, according to EPA data based on information submitted by the company. But Andrew Sherman, Terves’ founder and chief technical officer, disputed the figure, saying the company only emitted a fraction of that amount. Sherman did not respond to questions about whether the company plans to reduce its reliance on SF6.

Spartan Light Metal Products in Sparta, Illinois—one of the first magnesium casting companies to join the EPA’s SF6 emissions reduction partnership in the late 1990s—released 5.3 metric tons of SF6 in 2024. The company did not respond to requests for comment.

Auto manufacturers, the largest consumer of cast magnesium in the U.S., also had little to say.

This story is funded by readers like you.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Donate Now

Four of the top five leading carmakers in the United States—Ford, Toyota, General Motors and Stellantis—declined to comment about whether they consider suppliers’ use of SF6 when choosing manufacturers of magnesium parts.…

item.title: U.N. Climate Talks End Without a Deal Amid Rift Over Fossil Fuels
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: analysis of the COP31 negotiations and outcomes

For the first time in 17 years, the yearly U.N. climate conference ended without a deal. Negotiations in Antalya, Turkey, broke down as countries resisted a push by petrostates to omit mention of fossil fuels from the final agreement.

Objecting to the proposal were the E.U., much of Latin America, and vulnerable Pacific island nations. Speaking for the E.U., Irish environment minister Darragh O’Brien said it was “unconscionable that we would have a climate pact that makes no reference to fossil fuels.”

On the other side of the divide were major fossil fuel producers, led by Saudi Arabia and Russia. Some observers say the petrostates have grown more bold in climate negotiations in the absence of U.S. leadership. Since President Trump returned to office, the U.S. has moved to pull out of the U.N. climate treaty. It did not send an official delegation to Antalya.

The rejected agreement also had little say about climate reparations. In 2022, countries agreed to establish a fund to help poorer nations cope with climate disasters, but the draft deal included no firm commitments by wealthy countries to shore up the fund.

“We cannot afford another round of promises without meaningful action,” said former vice president Al Gore writing on X. Under the U.N. climate process, any agreement must be approved by consensus, meaning that every country, including major fossil fuel producers, effectively has veto power over the final text. Gore called for reforming the process “to stop polluters from blocking progress.”

In the 2015 Paris Agreement, nations set a goal of limiting warming to 1.5 degrees C. But according to a recent U.N. report the world is rapidly blowing past that threshold. Average global temperatures over the past three years were more than 1.5 degrees C warmer than the preindustrial era, and there is evidence that warming is accelerating.

As warming enters dangerous new territory, Bill Hare, head of think tank Climate Analytics, sees signs of hope in the failed agreement. “Countries committed to a safer future drew a line in the sand and refused to sign up to a document that did not include any reference to phasing out fossil fuels,” he said. Hare added, “That was clearly unacceptable, and countries that refused to accept it were right to do so.”

item.title: El Niño is already scrambling your ski season
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explains the impact of El Niño on the ski season

Being open for Thanksgiving has long been a goal for major ski resorts, including Sugarbush in Vermont. It had planned to have its lifts running and its slopes swarming by now. But with highs approaching 60 degrees Fahrenheit for much of the past week, that hasn’t happened.

”It’s been a really warm November,” said John Bleh, director of communications at Sugarbush. “New snowmaking technology has helped a ton, but it’s not the ultimate cure-all.”

The popular destination is one of a slew throughout the East, from Sugarloaf in Maine to Snowshoe Mountain in West Virginia, that have had to delay opening due to unseasonably balmy conditions.

On the other side of the country, skiers in California are gloating. Resorts in the Lake Tahoe area received more than 4 feet of snow after a recent series of storms. The bounty was so generous that the Sierra Avalanche Center was warning of a “considerable” risk of slides and Kirkwood Mountain Resort opened nearly two weeks ahead of schedule. “It’s always exciting to get the season underway, but being able to open this early is a huge win,” Ricky Newberry, the resort’s general manager, said in a statement.

It’s a bit more complicated in the Rockies. Some resorts in Utah and Colorado got off to a slow start before recent storms brought snow, but Wolf Creek in the southern end of the state has opened all of its terrain.

These wildly different starts to the ski season are a clear sign that the “super” or “Godzilla” El Niño, the strongest on record, is already shaping what could be a weird winter on the slopes.

El Niño occurs every three to five years when a band of unusually warm water forms off the coast of South America, altering weather patterns worldwide. The effects will vary widely: California is expected to be wetter than normal, the Northwest drier, and the Northeast wetter and warmer.

With El Niño’s impacts sticking around through March, the contrasts playing out at resorts right now may become more pronounced as winter settles in, said meteorologist Chris Tomer, who specializes in mountain and snow forecasting. “All roads run through the Sierra,” noted Tomer, referring to the Sierra Nevada mountain range. He expects the region’s resorts to receive 100 to 200 inches more snow than usual over the season. The Northeast will see its share of storms, but with temperatures expected to run warmer than normal, the question is whether that precipitation will fall as snow or rain.

“It’s a little off-putting at times,” said Bryan Rivard, who handles media relations at the trade group Ski Vermont. Still, he’s trying to remain optimistic. “If the weather comes, it could bring some pretty big stuff.”

In some ways, this year may be a repeat of 2015 and 2016, another “super” El Nino season that blessed the West and stressed the East. But as climate change accelerates warming patterns in general, the guarantee of skiable snow is increasingly difficult to come by even in normal years. That’s one reason that resorts have been investing millions of dollars in advanced snowmaking equipment.

“It’s enabling us to make snow in much tighter windows,” said Rivard. Modern snow guns and systems allow crews to work even when the temperatures dip for only a matter of hours. Bleh agrees that this has changed the dynamic considerably, but cautions against overreliance on the technology. “Every year we are making snowmaking upgrades,” he said. “But we need the temperatures to be able to do anything, and a long enough window to make it worth it.”

Those temperatures are set to arrive at Sugarbush this week, and the resort hopes to open by Thanksgiving or the day after. By then, some places in California will have seen nearly two weeks of skiing, an early glimpse of a winter that promises plenty of snow — just not where or when skiers might want it.

item.title: Climate Hope
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source. (Clean-up failed for this item, so the body is a truncated excerpt of the original.)

Why it is here: podcast summary with insights on climate progress

Welcome to Inside Climate, a podcast from the staff of Inside Climate News. Climate change and the environmental stress it can generate have made plenty of headlines this year. Our newsroom has covered floods, wildfires and heatwaves that have devastated communities across the globe. But amid the chaos, we’ve also witnessed moments of progress. In the spirit of Thanksgiving, co-host Kiley Price welcomes reporters Teresa Tomassoni and Katie Surma to discuss reef resilience and the rights of nature, respectively. And clean energy reporter Dan Gearino looks ahead, considering how the Democrats’ success in the midterm elections could lead to state action on climate policy.

Listen and subscribe on YouTube, Spotify, Apple Podcasts, Amazon Music, and iHeart.

KILEY PRICE

2026 has been a year of brutal climate realities, from record-high sea surface temperatures:

TERESA TOMASSONI: 96 percent of the world’s shallow coral reefs, including the Great Barrier Reef, others in the Coral Triangle and the Pacific, face a real risk of collapse in the next 50 years.

to deadly consequences for people protecting the environment.

KATIE SURMA: Last year in Brazil, environmental defenders, so those are people who peacefully act to protect nature, were killed at twice the level they were the year before.

But as Thanksgiving approaches, Inside Climate is highlighting stories that show progress on climate and environmental issues.

DAN GEARINO: I expect in the next two years to see major actions at the state level on climate policy.

TERESA TOMASSONI: Scientists around the world are striving to identify these super reefs.

KATIE SURMA: Ecuador became the only country in the world to recognize nature’s rights in its constitution.

That’s coming up on Inside Climate.

Welcome to this Thanksgiving edition of Inside Climate. I’m your host, Kiley Price.

The climate beat is constantly awash in negative news. From deadly heatwaves this summer to a glacier collapse that caused flash floods and killed thousands in Nepal, 2026 has been a stunning year for catastrophic climate events.

It’s easy to feel overwhelmed by these headlines.

So as Americans take a moment this week to pause and unite with friends and family for the Thanksgiving holiday, Inside Climate decided to check in with newsroom colleagues to hear about stories that provide hope and some good news for climate action.

We’ll begin with Dan Gearino to understand what the outcome of the midterm elections means for U.S. climate policy and clean energy.

Then, we’ll check in with oceans reporter Teresa Tomassoni about the latest research to protect coral reefs around the world.

And we’ll conclude with rights of nature reporter Katie Surma to get a sloth update and hear how Amazonian communities are fighting back against governments imposing oil projects on their territories.

Midterm Makeover

KILEY PRICE

Hi Dan, welcome back to the show.

DAN GEARINO

Great to be here.

KILEY PRICE

You are the author of the Inside Clean Energy newsletter at ICN, but you’ve also spent the last several months closely following key midterm races and ballot initiatives. Now that the midterms are behind us, what are some of the strongest climate wins that resulted from the election?

DAN GEARINO

So just the top line is that Democrats exceeded probably their very wildest expectations. And it is not a partisan statement to say that Democrats are a heck of a lot more likely to take action on climate, to take action that would reduce carbon emissions and also to support renewable energy. So Democrats won in places they didn’t expect to win, and it gives them a lot more control in the U.S. Congress and then also across the country in statehouses.

KILEY PRICE

What were some of those places?

DAN GEARINO

So one of the really big considerations if you’re looking at the state level is Democrats gaining trifectas. That means they win the governor’s race and they win both chambers of the legislature. Places that I expect to see significant changes as a result of new trifectas: Number one on my list is Wisconsin.

It’s been a while since there was a Wisconsin trifecta. Wisconsin has so much opportunity to do legislation that would encourage renewable energy. They have not really passed any major climate legislation. They are different from their kind of peer group in their neighborhood. Illinois passed major legislation, Michigan has, Minnesota has. Wisconsin’s just sitting there and it’s a wind-rich state.

Pennsylvania also has a new trifecta, and that seemed as if it was at the outer bounds of possible. This is a state that produces a tremendous amount of natural gas. If state policymakers even take baby steps toward acknowledging the effects of climate change, it would make a big difference because this is a state that is responsible for a ton of emissions.

Now if you look at the U.S. Congress, there were wins for Democrats in places that I don’t think a lot of people were expecting and what that means is you’ve got enough of a margin to pass things. The House majority looks like it’s gonna be gigantic, so you have that same issue. You can afford to have a bunch of Democrats not support certain legislation and you can still pass it. Now we’ve got President Trump, who’s going to veto just about everything that the Democratic majorities would want to do. But it is, it is this kind of important table setting what comes after. Because basically we’re in a world now where we are looking to 2028 and we’re kind of assembling the pieces on the board for what happens then.

item.title: Mongabay Kids launches Wild Guardians: A free education initiative to engage children with nature
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: initiative to engage children with nature

Mongabay Kids has launched Wild Guardians, a free multimedia educational series that connects upper elementary students with nature and inspires them to become stewards of wild things and wild places.

Wild Guardians features stories of children and young people around the world working to protect their favorite animals and ecosystems. Through fun five-minute-long videos, illustrated comics and standards-aligned lessons and activities for fourth and fifth graders, Wild Guardians aims to bridge the gap between storytelling and environmental stewardship.

The series features three different conservation topics: Restoring habitat for giraffes in Tanzania, the colorful world of wild bees and exploring and protecting waterways in Tennessee, U.S.

Here are the adventures Wild Guardians takes children on:

Follow a group of primary school students in Tanzania who are growing food for giraffes and their community. Children will learn about how they can support their own local wildlife through tree planting, cleanups and habitat restoration.

Exploring and protecting waterways

Elementary students in Chattanooga, Tennessee, explore their local creek and watershed, home to wildlife such as the hellbender and crawfish. Children will learn that waterways connect landscapes, from mountains to sea, how human activities affect freshwater ecosystems and what they can do to help care for local waterways and the wildlife that depend on them.

Students learn that there are more 20,000 species of bees, most of them wild bees that don’t produce honey. Children will go on a wild bee safari to learn about the importance of wild bees for pollination, how their habitat is being fragmented and what they can do to help.

“The great thing about the Wild Guardians resources is that students are learning about conservation in their local community alongside math, English language arts and social studies,” said Wild Guardians education lead Emily Townsend.

“Wild Guardians resources are versatile. The toolkits each focus on a different conservation topic and include a video, comic and interdisciplinary lessons. Teachers choose what works best for their classroom and all the resources are included to engage students as stewards of their community,” Townsend said.

“One of the things I find most meaningful about Wild Guardians is its potential to help children move from simply learning about wildlife and ecosystems to understanding that they can play an active role in protecting them. Children need opportunities to connect what they learn in the classroom with the places, species and environmental challenges around them,” said Mallory Lindsay of The Chuck & Ernestina Kreutzkamp Foundation’s Earth Focus Initiative, the primary funder of the Wild Guardians project.

“The Wild Guardians project provides a practical toolkit for kids to take action for nature. This gives kids a sense of hope,” said Veila Makundi and Monica Bond of the Wild Nature Institute, whose work is featured in the video about children in Tanzania growing food for giraffes and their community.
